title: The ground as a weapon
author: Weather Commons · historical study 02
description: Project Popeye, the Lao panhandle and the conversion of rain into a military instrument. October 1966 / January 1967.

source.title: ERA5 100 m wind · 1 October 1966, 00 UTC
source.license: ERA5 via Open-Meteo · attribution CC BY 4.0; Natural Earth public domain
source.note: A real reanalysis product, sampled from ERA5 via Open-Meteo on a 7×7 grid at 1° spacing. 100 m above-ground wind speed/direction converted to east/north components. The pilot freezes the 00 UTC field for its entire run, applies it over a smooth sphere and releases hypothetical tracers. This is not an aircraft flight, a reconstruction of a seeding mission or a rainfall-effect calculation. The archive establishes the month of testing, not this release date, point, altitude or size.

chapters.label: 01 / Archive
chapters.title: Rain enters the military plan.
chapters.text: A January 1967 memorandum records October 1966 tests in the Se Kong valley and proposes extending rain to obstruct transport. The document is evidence of intent and official claims; it does not independently establish effectiveness.

chapters.label: 02 / Architecture
chapters.title: A ford becomes a bottleneck.
chapters.text: The memorandum treats stream crossings, damaged bridges and roads as vulnerable infrastructure. It also anticipates risks to harvests and civilian movement. These are contemporary expectations, not measured outcomes in this visualization.

chapters.label: 03 / Inhabited ground
chapters.title: The war persists in the land.
chapters.text: UN reporting describes unexploded ordnance restricting agriculture and the construction of roads and schools in Laos. This is a documented legacy of bombing, distinct from the uncertain effects of weather modification.

chapters.label: 04 / Method
chapters.title: An archive is not a counterfactual.
chapters.text: Reanalysis estimates weather using observations and a numerical model. A wet day cannot, on its own, identify added rain from seeding. Our particle paths ask about sensitivity to an assumed field; they do not answer whether Popeye worked.
